clinicalPearls: A common secondary open-angle glaucoma caused by deposition of greyish-white fibrillar pseudoexfoliation material throughout the anterior segment that obstructs the trabecular meshwork
The classic lens sign is a central disc and a peripheral band of deposited material separated by a clear zone where the mobile iris wipes the surface
Deposits and pigment loss at the pupillary ruff, along with dense trabecular pigmentation on gonioscopy, are supportive signs, and dilation may reveal material on the lens periphery and zonules
It is a systemic elastic-tissue disorder linked to variants in the LOXL1 gene, with material also found in extraocular tissues
Zonular weakness is a hallmark, increasing the risk of lens subluxation, capsule rupture, and vitreous loss during cataract surgery, and phacodonesis may be visible
Intraocular pressure is often higher and more fluctuating than in primary open-angle glaucoma, so the disease can be more aggressive with poorer prognosis
Treatment lowers pressure with topical agents and laser trabeculoplasty, which often works well initially, with drainage surgery reserved for uncontrolled cases
Both eyes should be examined even when signs appear unilateral, as involvement is frequently asymmetric
reference.pathophysiology: Pseudoexfoliation is a generalised disorder of elastic microfibril metabolism, strongly associated with variants in the LOXL1 gene, in which abnormal greyish fibrillar material is produced and deposited in ocular and systemic tissues. In the eye this material accumulates on the anterior lens capsule, pupil margin, zonules, ciliary body, iris, and corneal endothelium. Material and liberated iris pigment progressively obstruct the trabecular meshwork and damage trabecular cells, reducing aqueous outflow and raising intraocular pressure, often with large fluctuations. Deposition also weakens the zonular apparatus, predisposing to lens instability. The optic nerve sustains glaucomatous damage that tends to progress more rapidly than in primary open-angle glaucoma.
additionalDifferentials: True exfoliation (capsular delamination) from heat or infrared exposure
Uveitic glaucoma with anterior segment deposits
Amyloid deposition in the anterior segment
additionalInvestigations: Dilated slit-lamp examination for the target-like lens deposits, pupillary ruff changes, and phacodonesis
Gonioscopy to assess trabecular pigmentation and exclude angle closure
Applanation tonometry with attention to pressure fluctuation
OCT of the retinal nerve fibre layer to quantify glaucomatous damage
Automated perimetry to monitor field loss
Assessment of zonular integrity before planning cataract surgery
redFlags: Very high or widely fluctuating intraocular pressure driving rapid optic-nerve damage
Phacodonesis or lens subluxation warning of high surgical risk from zonular weakness
Advanced field loss at presentation because the disease was under-recognised
Sudden pressure decompensation or angle closure from lens instability
reference.prognosis: Pseudoexfoliation glaucoma generally follows a more aggressive course than primary open-angle glaucoma, with higher and more variable pressures and faster progression, so close monitoring is needed; cataract surgery carries elevated risk from zonular weakness but may itself modestly lower pressure.
pitfalls: Failing to dilate the pupil and missing the peripheral lens deposits that confirm the diagnosis
Underestimating the aggressive pressure behaviour and monitoring too infrequently
Not anticipating zonular weakness and capsule instability during cataract surgery
Mistaking dense trabecular pigment for pigmentary glaucoma
Assuming the fellow eye is unaffected without examining it
management: Lower intraocular pressure with topical therapy, using a prostaglandin analogue first-line and adding beta-blockers, alpha-agonists or carbonic anhydrase inhibitors as required
Laser trabeculoplasty, which is often effective given the heavily pigmented trabecular meshwork
Incisional glaucoma surgery such as trabeculectomy or a drainage device for uncontrolled or progressive disease
Anticipate zonular weakness at cataract surgery, using a capsular tension ring and careful technique, and refer to an experienced surgeon
Frequent pressure monitoring given large diurnal fluctuations, with optical coherence tomography of the nerve fibre layer and automated perimetry to track progression
Treat to a lower target pressure, recognising the more aggressive course than primary open-angle glaucoma
Ophthalmology follow-up, mindful of the systemic elastic-tissue nature of the disorder
